title: MD Rules Committee Votes to Crack Down on Fake Law Citations Amid AI Use
author: Ian Round

dom.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition through a Maryland case in which counsel relied on a clerk’s AI-assisted drafting without personally checking the citations. It also reinforces the distinction between nonexistent authorities and genuine cases that do not support the cited proposition, and links the failure to existing duties of competence, supervision and meritorious advocacy rather than treating AI use itself as the violation.

kp.k: Proposed rule makes signatures certify citation verification
kp.d: The article reports that Maryland's Standing Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure unanimously voted to add language making an attorney's signature certify verification of every cited authority. As reported on March 20, 2026, the change still required adoption by the Maryland Supreme Court; it was not yet an operative rule.
qs: After a brief discussion in Annapolis, the rules committee decided unanimously to add language to an existing rule stating that an attorney's signature on a document means that they've verified every authority cited. The Maryland Supreme Court would have to adopt the change.

kp.k: Sanctions target willful fabrication, excluding self-represented litigants
kp.d: The proposed change explicitly addresses willful use of fake citations rather than creating a new prohibition on them. The article describes monetary sanctions as requiring an adverse party's motion seeking the costs of opposing a bad-faith pleading, and states that the rule would not apply to self-represented litigants.
qs: Fake citations have never been allowed, of course, but the rule makes it explicit that the "willful" use of them could result in sanctions.
The adverse party would have to file a motion requesting monetary sanctions for the cost of opposing a "bad faith" pleading. The rule would not apply to self-represented litigants.

kp.k: AI citation failures prompted clarification of existing duties
kp.d: The article reports increasing instances of attorneys filing generative-AI-written motions containing nonexistent cases or authorities that do not support the propositions cited, without quantifying the trend. The Maryland Appellate Court urged the change. Committee vice chair and Appellate Judge Douglas Nazarian framed it as a basic verification requirement consistent with longstanding obligations, not a prohibition on arguing about a case's meaning.
qs: Nazarian said the rule sets a "relatively low bar — does this case even exist?"

The committee, a function of the state Supreme Court, took up the change at the urging of the Maryland Appellate Court and comes as an increasing number of attorneys have filed motions written by generative artificial intelligence that cite cases that either don't exist or don't support the propositions for which they are cited.
"The whole point of lawyers is to fight about what a case *means*."

kp.k: Delegated ChatGPT drafting led to attorney disciplinary referral
kp.d: In the October case reported as Maryland appellate courts' first treatment of attorneys' improper AI use, Adam Hyman said his unlicensed, law-school-graduate clerk used ChatGPT to draft a divorce-case brief. He asked whether she had verified citations but did not verify them himself, acknowledging that he typically did not read cited cases. The court referred him to the Attorney Grievance Commission; Judge Kathryn Graeff described likely violations of competence, responsibility for employees' work, and meritorious-issues duties, rather than reporting a final disciplinary finding.
qs: The state's second-highest court in October referred a lawyer to the Attorney Grievance Commission and recommended that the rules committee or General Assembly consider taking action after he filed a motion "replete with citation irregularities."
He told the court that he asked the clerk — a law school graduate but not a licensed attorney — if she verified each citation, but he did not verify them himself.
He acknowledged that he typically does not read the cases he cites.

Graeff wrote that Hyman likely violated rules requiring competent representation, holding attorneys responsible for their employees' work and mandating that lawyers "bring or defend only meritorious issues."

kp.k: Corrective steps did not secure permission to replace authorities
kp.d: The court denied Hyman permission to amend the brief using real authorities. Graeff acknowledged preventive steps but criticized his lack of remorse for his failures and the additional work caused in the case, illustrating the reported consequences beyond the disciplinary referral.
qs: The court denied Hyman's request to amend the brief with real legal authorities.

Although Graeff acknowledged that Hyman had "taken steps" to prevent it from happening again, she wrote, "it would be a stretch to say that he was remorseful for his failures and the extra work that he caused in this case."

kp.k: Another court reprimanded lawyers for AI-generated fake cases
kp.d: The article reports that an Alabama federal judge reprimanded two Butler Snow lawyers the previous year for fake cases in an AI-generated filing. Both also represented Maryland in Baltimore jail-conditions litigation; one subsequently withdrew from that Maryland case, while the other remained listed as counsel. The article does not establish why the withdrawal occurred.
qs: In another case, an Alabama federal judge last year reprimanded two lawyers from the firm Butler Snow for citing fake cases in an AI-generated filing.
Those lawyers had also represented Maryland in a lawsuit over jail conditions in Baltimore. One of them withdrew from the Maryland case, while the other is still listed as representing the state.

kp.k: Bar guidance stresses verification and broader professional obligations
kp.d: The Maryland State Bar Association's May 2025 guidance emphasized human fact-checking and described obligations covering competent representation, client confidentiality, disclosure of generative AI use to clients, and reasonable fees. These are reported as bar guidance, distinct from the committee's proposed rule change.
qs: In guidance issued in May 2025, the Maryland State Bar Association stressed the importance of human fact-checking.
It noted that attorneys are obligated to provide competent representation, maintain client confidentiality, disclose the use of generative AI tools to clients and charge reasonable fees.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Round reports that AI-generated filings with nonexistent or unsupportive citations are prompting explicit verification requirements and disciplinary responses, rather than a new prohibition on fake citations.
pts.d: The article claims that an increasing number of attorneys have filed generative-AI-written motions containing citation problems. It reports a unanimous Maryland rules committee vote to make an attorney's signature certify verification of every cited authority, with potential sanctions for willful use of fake citations. This is a proposed change, not an operative rule. Judge Douglas Nazarian characterizes the verification threshold as basic confirmation that a case exists. Round also reports Maryland State Bar Association guidance emphasizing human fact-checking and lawyers' continuing duties when using generative AI. The source makes no quantified prediction about employment, productivity or legal-market restructuring.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of a committee decision, specific court incidents and professional guidance; the claimed increase in problematic filings is not quantified.
pts.d: Round describes the committee's discussion and unanimous vote. For concrete examples, he reports that Maryland's Appellate Court referred Adam Hyman to the Attorney Grievance Commission after a divorce-case filing with citation irregularities. Hyman told the court his clerk used ChatGPT and that he asked her about verification but did not verify the citations himself. Round attributes to Judge Kathryn Graeff the assessment that Hyman likely violated competence, employee-supervision and meritorious-issues obligations; this is not reported as a final disciplinary finding. A second example is an Alabama federal judge's reprimand of two Butler Snow lawyers for fake cases in an AI-generated filing. These are court incidents, not measured model hallucination rates or benchmark findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The March 20, 2026 report describes a pending rule change whose effectiveness depends on Maryland Supreme Court adoption and whose monetary-sanctions mechanism has specified conditions.
pts.d: The committee voted on the Friday of publication. The Maryland Supreme Court would still have to adopt the change. Round distinguishes existing prohibitions on fake citations from the proposal's explicit treatment of willful use. Monetary sanctions would require an adverse party's motion seeking the cost of opposing a bad-faith pleading. Self-represented litigants would be excluded. The Maryland referral is dated to the preceding October, the Alabama reprimand to the previous year, and the bar guidance to May 2025. The article gives no adoption deadline or forecast of the proposal's effectiveness.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The reported effects concern filing attorneys, supervised staff, opposing parties and clients; self-represented litigants are expressly outside the proposed rule.
pts.d: Attorneys signing filings would explicitly certify citation verification and could face sanctions under the stated conditions. The Hyman incident illustrates that delegating AI-assisted drafting to an unlicensed clerk does not remove the supervising lawyer's responsibility, according to Graeff's reported assessment. Opposing parties incur work responding to defective filings and could request monetary sanctions. Clients are affected through the professional duties identified in the bar association's guidance: competence, confidentiality, disclosure of generative-AI use and reasonable fees. The reported incidents span a divorce representation and a federal filing by law-firm lawyers; the article does not claim effects across particular firm sizes or the legal labour market.
